concepts: Evaluation of inverse trigonometric expressions (tan⁻¹ and sec⁻¹)
questions.question: $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1+\sqrt3}{3+\sqrt3}\right)+\sec^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{8+4\sqrt3}{6+3\sqrt3}}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Both surds collapse: $\frac{1+\sqrt3}{3+\sqrt3}=\frac1{\sqrt3}$ and the radicand is a perfect square ratio, so each term is a standard angle.
solution: Write $3+\sqrt3=\sqrt3(\sqrt3+1)$ and multiply the numerator and denominator under the root by $2$: $E=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1+\sqrt3}{\sqrt3(\sqrt3+1)}\right)+\sec^{-1}\left(\frac{16+8\sqrt3}{12+6\sqrt3}\right)^{1/2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Cancel the common factor $2+\sqrt3$ instead of squaring: the radicand is $\frac{4(2+\sqrt3)}{3(2+\sqrt3)}=\frac43$, and $\sec\theta=\frac2{\sqrt3}$ gives $\tan\theta=\frac1{\sqrt3}$.
solution: $8+4\sqrt3=4(2+\sqrt3)$ and $6+3\sqrt3=3(2+\sqrt3)$, so the radicand is $\frac43$ and $\sec^{-1}\sqrt{\frac43}=\sec^{-1}\frac2{\sqrt3}$.

useful_results: For $|y|\ge1$: $\sec^{-1}y=\cos^{-1}\frac1y$ and $\mathrm{cosec}^{-1}y=\sin^{-1}\frac1y$ (principal values).
For $\theta$ in the first quadrant, $\sec\theta=s\Rightarrow\tan\theta=\sqrt{s^2-1}$; here $s=\frac2{\sqrt3}\Rightarrow\tan\theta=\frac1{\sqrt3}$.
Look for a common factor ($2+\sqrt3$ here) before rationalising or squaring: surd ratios in JEE usually collapse to a simple number.

concepts: Addition and subtraction formulas for tan⁻¹
Principal value of sin⁻¹(sin x) and cos⁻¹(cos x)
questions.question: If $\sin^{-1}\frac{\alpha}{17}+\cos^{-1}\frac45-\tan^{-1}\frac{77}{36}=0$, $0<\alpha<13$, then $\sin^{-1}(\sin\alpha)+\cos^{-1}(\cos\alpha)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Reduce to $\sin^{-1}\frac\alpha{17}=\sin^{-1}\frac8{17}$ to get $\alpha=8$, then reduce $8$ rad into the principal ranges by subtracting $2\pi$ and reflecting.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take the sine of both sides as a right-triangle subtraction ($36$-$77$-$85$ and $3$-$4$-$5$ triangles) instead of using the $\tan^{-1}$ difference formula.
solution: Let $\theta=\sin^{-1}\frac\alpha{17}=A-B$ where $\tan A=\frac{77}{36}$ and $\cos B=\frac45$. The triangle $36,77,85$ gives $\sin A=\frac{77}{85},\cos A=\frac{36}{85}$; the triangle $3,4,5$ gives $\sin B=\frac35$.

useful_results: $\tan^{-1}a-\tan^{-1}b=\tan^{-1}\frac{a-b}{1+ab}$ whenever $ab>-1$; with Pythagorean triples ($3,4,5$; $8,15,17$; $36,77,85$) the angles can be read as triangles.
$\sin^{-1}(\sin x)=x-2k\pi$ if $x-2k\pi\in\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$, and $=(2k+1)\pi-x$ if $x\in\left[2k\pi+\frac\pi2,2k\pi+\frac{3\pi}2\right]$.
$\cos^{-1}(\cos x)$ is the $2\pi$-periodic triangular wave equal to the distance from $x$ to the nearest multiple of $2\pi$.
For $x\in\left[\frac{5\pi}{2},3\pi\right]$ the two terms $\sin^{-1}(\sin x)+\cos^{-1}(\cos x)=(3\pi-x)+(x-2\pi)=\pi$ for all such $x$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Telescoping sum of tan⁻¹ terms
Arithmetic progression of natural numbers
questions.question: Let $a_1=1,a_2,a_3,a_4,\dots$ be consecutive natural numbers. Then $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac1{1+a_1a_2}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac1{1+a_2a_3}\right)+\dots+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac1{1+a_{2021}a_{2022}}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Because consecutive terms differ by $1$, each $\frac1{1+a_ka_{k+1}}$ is $\frac{a_{k+1}-a_k}{1+a_ka_{k+1}}$, i.e. $\tan^{-1}a_{k+1}-\tan^{-1}a_k$, and the sum telescopes.
solution: The sum telescopes to $\tan^{-1}a_{2022}-\tan^{-1}a_1=\tan^{-1}2022-\tan^{-1}1=\tan^{-1}2022-\frac\pi4$, which is option (A).
Also $\tan^{-1}2022=\frac\pi2-\cot^{-1}2022$, so the sum $=\frac\pi2-\cot^{-1}2022-\frac\pi4=\frac\pi4-\cot^{-1}2022$, which is option (B).
Options (C) and (D) have the opposite sign and are wrong. Answer: (A) and (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF labels the two matching options 'Option 3' and 'Option 1' (numbering of the original JEE paper); in this paper's printed order they are (A) and (B). Working unchanged; answer (A, B) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complex numbers: $1+k(k+1)+i=(1-ik)(1+i(k+1))$, so each angle is $\arg(1+i(k+1))-\arg(1+ik)$ and the product of the complex numbers telescopes.
solution: The argument of $1+k(k+1)+i$ is $\tan^{-1}\frac1{1+k(k+1)}$ (positive real part). Arguments add under multiplication, so $\tan^{-1}\frac1{1+k(k+1)}=\arg(1+i(k+1))-\arg(1+ik)=\tan^{-1}(k+1)-\tan^{-1}k$.
$\arg(1+2022i)=\tan^{-1}2022$ and $\arg(1+i)=\frac\pi4$, so the sum is $\tan^{-1}2022-\frac\pi4$, i.e. (A) and, using $\tan^{-1}2022=\frac\pi2-\cot^{-1}2022$, also (B).

useful_results: $\tan^{-1}\frac{d}{1+a(a+d)}=\tan^{-1}(a+d)-\tan^{-1}a$ for $a(a+d)>-1$: the standard telescoper for an A.P. with common difference $d$.
The argument of a product of complex numbers is the sum of the arguments, so $\tan^{-1}$ sums can be seen as $\arg\prod(1+ia_k)$.

concepts: Principal value of sin⁻¹(sin θ) and inequalities
Range of sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹ (sin⁻¹t+cos⁻¹t=π/2)
questions.question: Let $(a,b)\subset(0,2\pi)$ be the largest interval for which $\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta)-\cos^{-1}(\sin\theta)>0$, $\theta\in(0,2\pi)$, holds. If $\alpha x^2+\beta x+\sin^{-1}(x^2-6x+10)+\cos^{-1}(x^2-6x+10)=0$ and $\alpha-\beta=b-a$, then $\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $x^2-6x+10=(x-3)^2+1\ge1$ while $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$ need the argument $\le1$, so $x=3$ is forced and the sum of the two inverse functions is $\frac\pi2$.
solution: Both inverse functions are defined only if $(x-3)^2+1\le1$, i.e. $x=3$; then each argument is $1$ and $\sin^{-1}1+\cos^{-1}1=\frac\pi2+0=\frac\pi2$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF jumps to 'x = 3' without saying why; the reason (the argument $(x-3)^2+1\ge1$ must equal $1$ for the inverse functions to exist) was added. Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Read $\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta)$ off its zig-zag graph piece by piece, instead of passing to $\sin\theta>\frac1{\sqrt2}$.
solution: Piece 1: $\theta>\frac\pi4$ gives $\left(\frac\pi4,\frac\pi2\right]$. Piece 2: $\pi-\theta>\frac\pi4$ gives $\theta<\frac{3\pi}4$, so $\left[\frac\pi2,\frac{3\pi}4\right)$. Piece 3: $\theta-2\pi\le0<\frac\pi4$, none.
Union: $\left(\frac\pi4,\frac{3\pi}4\right)$, so $b-a=\frac\pi2$; the rest ($x=3$, $\alpha=\frac\pi{12}$) is as before.

useful_results: $\sin^{-1}t+\cos^{-1}t=\frac\pi2$ for $t\in[-1,1]$, so $\cos^{-1}(\sin\theta)=\frac\pi2-\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta)$ for every real $\theta$.
A quadratic like $(x-h)^2+1$ fed into $\sin^{-1}$ or $\cos^{-1}$ forces its minimum point: the domain is the single point $x=h$.
$\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta)>c$ with $0<c<\frac\pi2$ holds exactly when $\theta\in(c,\pi-c)$ modulo $2\pi$.
If the domain collapses to a point, substitute that point to turn an apparently hard equation in $x$ into a linear relation between the parameters.

concepts: Range of inverse trigonometric functions (empty solution set)
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of all solutions of the equation $\cos^{-1}(2x)-2\cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)=\pi$, $x\in\left[-\frac12,\frac12\right]$. Then $\sum_{x\in S}2\sin^{-1}\left(x^2-1\right)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The left side can reach $\pi$ only if $\cos^{-1}(2x)=\pi$ and $\cos^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^2}=0$ at the same time, which needs $x=-\frac12$ and $x=0$: so $S=\varnothing$ and the sum is $0$.
solution: The range of $\cos^{-1}(2x)$ is $[0,\pi]$, while $2\cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)\ge0$, so the right side is $\ge\pi$.
$\cos^{-1}(2x)=\pi$ gives $x=-\frac12$, and $\cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)=0$ gives $x=0$: not possible together. Hence $S=\varnothing$.
A sum over the empty set is $0$, so $\sum_{x\in S}2\sin^{-1}(x^2-1)=0$, option (A).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's own working ends with 'sum over an empty set is 0', i.e. option (A) $0$, but its answer key prints (C). Option (C) $-\frac{2\pi}3$ is wrong: numerically the left side never exceeds $\frac{2\pi}3<\pi$ on $\left[-\frac12,\frac12\right]$, so $S$ is empty. Correct answer: (A) $0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $x=\sin\varphi$ so $\cos^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^2}=|\varphi|$, and bound the left side by $\pi-2|\varphi|$.
solution: But $\cos^{-1}(2\sin\varphi)\le\pi$, so the left side is $\le\pi-2|\varphi|\le\pi$, with equality only if $\varphi=0$ and $\cos^{-1}(0)=\pi$.
At $\varphi=0$, $\cos^{-1}(0)=\frac\pi2\ne\pi$. So there is no solution, $S=\varnothing$ and the sum is $0$.

useful_results: An equation $f(x)=g(x)$ in which one side is bounded above by $M$ and the other bounded below by $M$ holds only when both attain $M$: check whether they do at the same $x$.
A sum (or product) over an empty solution set is $0$ (or $1$): never skip the check that $S$ is non-empty.

concepts: Identities for 2tan⁻¹ and cos⁻¹ of (1−x²)/(1+x²)
Substitution x = tan θ
questions.question: Let $S=\left\{x\in\mathbb R:0<x<1\text{ and }2\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}\right)\right\}$. If $n(S)$ denotes the number of elements in $S$ then :
options: $n(S)=2$ and only one element in $S$ is less than $\frac12$.
$n(S)=1$ and the element in $S$ is less than $\frac12$.
$n(S)=1$ and the elements in $S$ is more than $\frac12$.
questions.key_idea: With $x=\tan\theta$, $\frac{1-x}{1+x}=\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)$ and $\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}=\cos2\theta$, both inside the principal ranges.
solution: $x=\tan\frac\pi8=\sqrt2-1\approx0.414$, which lies in $(0,1)$ and is less than $\frac12$.
So $n(S)=1$ and the element is less than $\frac12$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the identity $\cos^{-1}\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}=2\tan^{-1}x$ ($x\ge0$) so the equation reduces to equal $\tan^{-1}$'s.

useful_results: $\tan^{-1}\frac{1-x}{1+x}=\frac\pi4-\tan^{-1}x$ for $x>-1$.

A trig substitution $x=\tan\theta$ turns every $\frac{1\pm x}{1\mp x}$, $\frac{2x}{1-x^2}$, $\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}$ into $\tan(\frac\pi4\mp\theta),\tan2\theta,\cos2\theta$; always check the resulting angle against the principal range.

concepts: Parabola: focus and directrix
Domain restrictions of sin⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ identities
questions.question: Let $y=f(x)$ represent a parabola with focus $\left(-\frac12,0\right)$ and directrix $y=-\frac12$. Then $S=\left\{x\in\mathbb R:\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{f(x)}\right)+\sin^{-1}\left(\sqrt{f(x)+1}\right)=\frac\pi2\right\}$ :
questions.key_idea: $\sin^{-1}\sqrt{f+1}$ needs $f\le0$ and $\tan^{-1}\sqrt f$ needs $f\ge0$, so $f(x)=0$; equivalently $\tan^{-1}\sqrt f=\cos^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt{1+f}}$ leads to $f+1=1$.
solution: For a point $(x,y)$ on the parabola, distance from the focus equals distance from the directrix: $\sqrt{\left(x+\frac12\right)^2+y^2}=\left|y+\frac12\right|$.
$\tan^{-1}\sqrt{f(x)}=\cos^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt{1+f(x)}}$ (right triangle with legs $\sqrt f$ and $1$, defined for $f\ge0$).
The equation becomes $\cos^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt{1+f}}+\sin^{-1}\sqrt{f+1}=\frac\pi2$, and since $\cos^{-1}t+\sin^{-1}t=\frac\pi2$ this means $\sqrt{f+1}=\frac1{\sqrt{1+f}}$.
Both values check: $\tan^{-1}0+\sin^{-1}1=\frac\pi2$. So $S$ has exactly two elements: option (C).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the parabola as 'x²+x+y = f(x)' (a slip); expanding gives $y=x^2+x$, so $f(x)=x^2+x$. Everything after that is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the domains first: $\sqrt{f}$ needs $f\ge0$ and $\sin^{-1}\sqrt{f+1}$ needs $f+1\le1$, so $f=0$ at once, with no identity needed.
solution: $\sin^{-1}\sqrt{f(x)+1}$ is defined only if $0\le f(x)+1\le1$, i.e. $f(x)\le0$.

useful_results: Locus of a parabola from focus $(p,q)$ and horizontal directrix $y=k$: $(x-p)^2+(y-q)^2=(y-k)^2$ - expand and the $y^2$ terms cancel.
A domain argument can decide an equation before any algebra: $\sqrt{u}$ needs $u\ge0$ and $\sin^{-1}\sqrt{u+1}$ needs $u\le0$, so $u=0$.
$\tan^{-1}a=\cos^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt{1+a^2}}$ for $a\ge0$.

concepts: tan⁻¹ and cot⁻¹ identities with branch (x>0 and x<0)
Sum of roots of an equation
questions.question: If the sum of all the solutions of $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2x}{1-x^2}\right)+\cot^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^2}{2x}\right)=\frac\pi3$, $-1<x<1$, $x\ne0$, is $\alpha-\frac4{\sqrt3}$, then $\alpha$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\cot^{-1}y$ equals $\tan^{-1}\frac1y$ for $y>0$ but $\pi+\tan^{-1}\frac1y$ for $y<0$, so the cases $x>0$ and $x<0$ must be treated separately.
questions.correction_note: PDF solution gives only the final roots of each case; the intermediate quadratics were written out and the roots checked. Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $x=\tan\theta$ with $\theta\in\left(-\frac\pi4,\frac\pi4\right)$: the two arguments become $\tan2\theta$ and $\cot2\theta$.

useful_results: $\cot^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\frac1y$ for $y>0$ and $\pi+\tan^{-1}\frac1y$ for $y<0$ (range of $\cot^{-1}$ is $(0,\pi)$).
$\tan^{-1}\frac{2x}{1-x^2}=2\tan^{-1}x$ for $|x|<1$; it equals $2\tan^{-1}x\pm\pi$ outside.
Whenever $\frac{2x}{1-x^2}$ and $\frac{1-x^2}{2x}$ appear, $x=\tan\theta$ turns them into $\tan2\theta,\cot2\theta$.
Solutions found in each branch must be checked against that branch's own interval ($-\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt3$ were rejected here).

concepts: Domain of sin⁻¹(log base) with logarithm and exponential inequalities
Fractional part function and its range
questions.question: Let $D$ be the domain of the function $f(x)=\sin^{-1}\left(\log_{3x}\left(\frac{6+2\log_3x}{-5x}\right)\right)$. If the range of the function $g:D\to\mathbb R$ defined by $g(x)=x-[x]$ ($[x]$ is the greatest integer function), is $(\alpha,\beta)$, then $\alpha^2+\frac5\beta$ is equal to :
questions.answer: (D) $135$ (no key in the PDF; see the note: the exact value $\approx136.5$ matches no option)
questions.key_idea: The base $3x$ must be positive and $\ne1$, the quotient positive (so $x<\frac1{27}$), and $-1\le\log_{3x}(\cdot)\le1$ for base $<1$ means $3x\le(\cdot)\le\frac1{3x}$; then $g(x)=x$ on $D\subset(0,1)$.
solution: The argument of the logarithm must be positive: $\frac{6+2\log_3x}{-5x}>0$ with $x>0$ gives $6+2\log_3x<0\Rightarrow\log_3x<-3\Rightarrow x<\frac1{27}$.
So $0<x<\frac1{27}$ and the base $3x\in\left(0,\frac19\right)$ is less than $1$.
$\sin^{-1}$ needs $-1\le\log_{3x}\left(\frac{6+2\log_3x}{-5x}\right)\le1$; for a base less than $1$ this means $3x\le\frac{6+2\log_3x}{-5x}\le\frac1{3x}$.
Together with $x<\frac1{27}$ the domain is $D=[3^{-23/6},x_0]$ with $0<3^{-23/6}<x_0<\frac1{27}$, so $D\subset(0,1)$ and $[x]=0$.
Therefore $g(x)=x$ and the range of $g$ is $D$ itself: $\alpha=3^{-23/6}$ and $\beta$ is the right end of $D$.
Taking the right end as $\frac1{27}$ (the bound from $x<\frac1{27}$, the $15x^2$ term being negligible) gives $\alpha^2+\frac5\beta\approx3^{-23/3}+135\approx135$: option (D).
questions.correction_note: The PDF has no answer (the key is blank) and its solution is cut off after 'Range g(x) is domain of f(x)'. Written out in full. Rigorous check: the exact right end $x_0$ solves $x=3^{-3-7.5x^2}$, $x_0\approx0.03663$, so the exact value is $\alpha^2+\frac5\beta\approx136.50$, which matches no option (options 135 and 136 are both about 0.5 away); also the range is a closed interval, not $(\alpha,\beta)$. The question is flawed; (D) $135$ is the value obtained when the upper end is taken as $\frac1{27}$. Please review.
useful_results: For $\log_b t\in[-1,1]$: if $b>1$ then $\frac1b\le t\le b$; if $0<b<1$ then $b\le t\le\frac1b$.
Multiplying an inequality by a negative quantity (here $-5x$) reverses it - the commonest slip in such domain problems.
$x-[x]=\{x\}$, and for $x\in[0,1)$ it is simply $x$: the range of $\{x\}$ over a subset of $[0,1)$ is that subset.
Always check that a stated answer is consistent with the exact domain: here the closed interval and the approximate 135 signal a flawed question.

concepts: Range of sin⁻¹ composite function
questions.question: The range of $f(x)=4\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x^2}{x^2+1}\right)$ is :
questions.key_idea: $\frac{x^2}{x^2+1}=1-\frac1{x^2+1}$ takes every value in $[0,1)$ but never $1$, so $\sin^{-1}$ takes $[0,\frac\pi2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compose monotone pieces: $t=x^2\in[0,\infty)$, then $\frac t{1+t}$ increases from $0$ to $1$ (never reaching it), then $4\sin^{-1}$ increases.
solution: As $x$ runs over $\mathbb R$, $t=x^2$ takes every value in $[0,\infty)$.
$h(t)=\frac t{1+t}$ is continuous and strictly increasing with $h(0)=0$ and $h(t)\to1$ as $t\to\infty$, never equal to $1$: its range is $[0,1)$.
$4\sin^{-1}$ is continuous and increasing on $[0,1)$, so the range is $[4\sin^{-1}0,\ 4\sin^{-1}1)=[0,2\pi)$ with the upper end excluded.

useful_results: $\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}=1-\frac1{1+x^2}\in[0,1)$ for real $x$; likewise $\frac1{1+x^2}\in(0,1]$ and $\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\in[-1,1]$.
Range of a composite of continuous increasing functions is the image of the end points; check whether each end is attained (closed or open).
Related: range of $\tan^{-1}\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}$ is $\left[0,\frac\pi4\right)$ and of $\cos^{-1}\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ is $\left[0,\frac\pi2\right)$.

concepts: Domain of logarithmic and inverse trigonometric functions
questions.question: If the domain of the function $f(x)=\log_e\left(4x^2+11x+6\right)+\sin^{-1}(4x+3)+\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{10x+6}3\right)$ is $(\alpha,\beta]$, then $36|\alpha+\beta|$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Intersect three conditions: $4x^2+11x+6>0$, $|4x+3|\le1$ and $\left|\frac{10x+6}3\right|\le1$; the strict inequality gives the open left end.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $t=4x+3$: every condition becomes a condition on $t$, and the logarithm's quadratic factors as $t(x+2)$ with $x+2>0$ automatic.
solution: $\sin^{-1}t$ needs $-1\le t\le1$; then $t+5>0$, so $\log_e$ needs $t>0$. Hence $0<t\le1$.
$\frac{10x+6}3=\frac{5t-3}{6}$, and $-1\le\frac{5t-3}6\le1\Leftrightarrow-\frac35\le t\le\frac95$, which holds for all $t\in(0,1]$.

useful_results: Domain problems: write each function's requirement as an inequality, solve each on a number line and intersect; strict inequalities (logs, denominators) give open ends, inverse-trig bounds give closed ends.
A linear substitution $t=ax+b$ matching the inverse-trig argument often decouples the conditions.
$\log_e(\text{quadratic})$: factor the quadratic and test the sign of each factor on the interval left by the inverse-trig conditions.

concepts: Domain of logarithmic and cos⁻¹ functions
Rational inequalities (wavy curve method)
questions.question: If the domain of the function $\log_e\left(\frac{6x^2+5x+1}{2x-1}\right)+\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{2x^2-3x+4}{3x-5}\right)$ is $(\alpha,\beta)\cup(\gamma,\delta]$, then $18\left(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2\right)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Solve $\frac{(3x+1)(2x+1)}{2x-1}>0$ and $\left|\frac{2x^2-3x+4}{3x-5}\right|\le1$ (split as two inequalities) and intersect on a number line.

alternate_solutions.idea: Replace $\left|\frac{2x^2-3x+4}{3x-5}\right|\le1$ by the difference of squares: $(2x^2-3x+4)^2\le(3x-5)^2$, which factors and avoids sign charts with a denominator.
solution: $2x^2-6x+9>0$ always (discriminant $<0$), so $2x^2-1\le0$, i.e. $-\frac1{\sqrt2}\le x\le\frac1{\sqrt2}$ (and $x\ne\frac53$ holds automatically).

useful_results: $|P|\le|Q|\iff(P-Q)(P+Q)\le0$ (with $Q\ne0$ where it is a denominator): turns an absolute-value bound on a fraction into a polynomial inequality.
$\cos^{-1}R$ or $\sin^{-1}R$ needs $|R|\le1$, i.e. two inequalities that are best combined by squaring.
A quadratic with negative discriminant and positive leading coefficient is always positive: drop it from sign charts.

concepts: Domain of sec⁻¹ (|y| ≥ 1)
Rational inequalities
questions.question: If the domain of the function $f(x)=\sec^{-1}\left(\frac{2x}{5x+3}\right)$ is $[\alpha,\beta)\cup(\gamma,\delta]$, then $|3\alpha+10(\beta+\gamma)+21\delta|$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\sec^{-1}y$ needs $|y|\ge1$: solve $\frac{2x}{5x+3}\ge1$ and $\frac{2x}{5x+3}\le-1$ separately and read the end points.

alternate_solutions.idea: $|y|\ge1\iff y^2\ge1$: square, factor as a difference of squares and get a single quadratic inequality (no case split).

useful_results: $\sec^{-1}y$ and $\mathrm{cosec}^{-1}y$ have domain $|y|\ge1$ (i.e. $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$); $\cot^{-1}$ and $\tan^{-1}$ have domain $\mathbb R$.
$|y|\ge1\iff y^2\ge1$: squaring removes the case split and the denominator sign problem ($x=-\frac35$ is excluded separately).
The hole $x=-\frac35$ explains why the answer is written as a union with $\beta=\gamma$.

concepts: tan⁻¹ difference formula and sin⁻¹ of a right-triangle ratio
Evaluating trigonometric values at multiples of π/2
questions.question: If $S=\left\{x\in\mathbb R:\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+2}}\right)-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\right)=\frac\pi4\right\}$, then $\sum_{x\in S}\left(\sin\left((x^2+x+5)\frac\pi2\right)-\cos\left((x^2+x+5)\pi\right)\right)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{(x+1)^2+1}}$ is the sine of $\tan^{-1}(x+1)$, so the equation is $\tan^{-1}(x+1)-\tan^{-1}x=\frac\pi4$, giving $x^2+x=0$.
solution: $\sin^{-1}\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+2}}=\tan^{-1}(x+1)$ and $\sin^{-1}\frac x{\sqrt{x^2+1}}=\tan^{-1}x$ (both arguments are $\sin$ of $\tan^{-1}$), so the equation is $\tan^{-1}(x+1)-\tan^{-1}x=\frac\pi4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complex numbers: the left side is $\arg(1+i(x+1))-\arg(1+ix)=\arg\frac{1+i(x+1)}{1+ix}$, whose argument is $\frac\pi4$ exactly when real part equals imaginary part.
solution: This argument is $\frac\pi4$ iff real part $=$ imaginary part (both positive): $1+x+x^2=1\Rightarrow x=0,-1$.
At each, $x^2+x+5=5$ and the term is $\sin\frac{5\pi}2-\cos5\pi=2$; the sum over the two elements is $4$.

useful_results: $\frac{u}{\sqrt{1+u^2}}=\sin(\tan^{-1}u)$ and $\frac1{\sqrt{1+u^2}}=\cos(\tan^{-1}u)$, so $\sin^{-1}\frac u{\sqrt{1+u^2}}=\tan^{-1}u$ for all real $u$.
Angle between lines or arguments: $\tan^{-1}a-\tan^{-1}b=\tan^{-1}\frac{a-b}{1+ab}$ for $ab>-1$.
$\sin\left(n\frac\pi2\right)$ and $\cos(n\pi)$ for integer $n$: $\sin\frac{5\pi}2=1$, $\cos5\pi=-1$ (period $2\pi$, so $5\equiv1$ mod $4$ and mod $2$).

concepts: Number of solutions of an inverse trigonometric equation
Double-angle formula for sin and tan⁻¹ substitution
questions.question: For $x\in(-1,1]$, the number of solutions of the equation $\sin^{-1}x=2\tan^{-1}x$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Take $\sin$ of both sides to get $x=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}$, then check each candidate in the original equation.
solution: Check: $x=0$: $0=0$. $x=1$: $\sin^{-1}1=\frac\pi2=2\tan^{-1}1$. Both satisfy the original equation.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $\theta=\tan^{-1}x\in\left(-\frac\pi4,\frac\pi4\right]$ so that $2\theta$ stays in the principal range of $\sin^{-1}$, and $x=\tan\theta$ becomes $\tan\theta=\sin2\theta$.
solution: Let $\theta=\tan^{-1}x\in\left(-\frac\pi4,\frac\pi4\right]$ (since $x\in(-1,1]$). Then $2\theta\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$, so $\sin^{-1}x=2\theta$ means $x=\sin2\theta$ exactly (no extra branch).
$\sin\theta=0$ gives $\theta=0$; $\cos^2\theta=\frac12$ gives $\theta=\pm\frac\pi4$, of which $\theta=\frac\pi4$ is allowed ($\theta=-\frac\pi4$ means $x=-1$, excluded).

useful_results: For $|x|\le1$: $\sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{1+x^2}=2\tan^{-1}x$, so $\sin^{-1}x=2\tan^{-1}x$ means $x=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}$ only when $2\tan^{-1}x$ stays in $\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$ - true exactly for $|x|\le1$.
When you take $\sin$ (or $\tan$) of both sides, you can create extra roots: always test candidates in the original equation and against the stated interval.
Substituting $\theta=\tan^{-1}x$ makes the range of $2\theta$ visible immediately.

concepts: tan⁻¹ addition formula and quadratic equation
Principal values and positivity
questions.question: Considering only the principal values of inverse trigonometric functions, the number of positive real values of $x$ satisfying $\tan^{-1}(x)+\tan^{-1}(2x)=\frac\pi4$ is :
questions.key_idea: For $x>0$ move one term across, take $\tan$, and solve the quadratic $2x^2+3x-1=0$; only one root is positive.
solution: Only $x=\frac{-3+\sqrt{17}}4\approx0.28>0$ is possible (and $2x\cdot x<1$ so the formula is valid). Hence exactly one positive value: option (A).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $x=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt{9+8}}{8}$; the denominator should be $2a=4$, so $x=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt{17}}4$. The count of positive roots (one) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Monotonicity: for $x>0$ the left side is continuous and strictly increasing, starting below $\frac\pi4$ and ending above it, so it equals $\frac\pi4$ exactly once - no solving needed.
solution: $h(x)=\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}2x$ has $h'(x)=\frac1{1+x^2}+\frac2{1+4x^2}>0$, so $h$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.
By the intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity, $h(x)=\frac\pi4$ has exactly one positive solution: option (A).

useful_results: For $a,b>0$ with $ab<1$: $\tan^{-1}a+\tan^{-1}b=\tan^{-1}\frac{a+b}{1-ab}$; with $ab>1$ add $\pi$.
Counting solutions of an equation $f(x)=c$ is often faster by monotonicity (sum of increasing functions) than by solving.

concepts: Double-angle identity cos(2 sin⁻¹x)
Quadratic equation: roots and the line through a point
questions.question: Let $x=\frac mn$ ($m,n$ are co-prime natural numbers) be a solution of the equation $\cos\left(2\sin^{-1}x\right)=\frac19$ and let $\alpha,\beta$ ($\alpha>\beta$) be the roots of the equation $mx^2-nx-m+n=0$. Then the point $(\alpha,\beta)$ lies on the line :
questions.key_idea: $\cos(2\sin^{-1}x)=1-2x^2$ gives $x=\frac23$, so $m=2,n=3$ and the quadratic is $2x^2-3x+1=0$ with roots $1$ and $\frac12$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The coefficients of $mx^2-nx-m+n$ add to $0$, so $x=1$ is always a root and the other root is found from the product of roots, with no formula.
solution: For $mx^2-nx-m+n$ the coefficient sum is $m-n-m+n=0$, so $x=1$ is a root; the product of roots is $\frac{-m+n}{m}=\frac12$, so the other root is $\frac12$.
Since $\alpha>\beta$: $\alpha=1,\beta=\frac12$, and the point $\left(1,\frac12\right)$ lies on $5x+8y=9$: option (A).

useful_results: If the coefficients of $ax^2+bx+c$ add to zero, $x=1$ is a root and the other root is $\frac ca$.
Always use the sign information ($m,n$ natural numbers) to pick the right sign of $x$.

concepts: Domain of cos⁻¹ with modulus and of a reciprocal logarithm
questions.question: If the domain of the function $f(x)=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{2-|x|}4\right)+\left\{\log_e(3-x)\right\}^{-1}$ is $[-\alpha,\beta)-\{\gamma\}$, then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $|2-|x||\le4$ gives $|x|\le6$; the reciprocal logarithm needs $3-x>0$ and $\ln(3-x)\ne0$, i.e. $x<3$ and $x\ne2$.
useful_results: $\cos^{-1}\frac{a-|x|}{b}$ has domain $|a-|x||\le b$, i.e. $|x|\le a+b$ whenever $a-b\le0$ (here $-2\le|x|$ is vacuous).
A reciprocal $\frac1{g(x)}$ removes the zeros of $g$; a logarithm $\ln u$ is zero at $u=1$.
Here the braces are plain brackets, not a fractional part: $\{\log_e(3-x)\}^{-1}=\frac1{\log_e(3-x)}$.

concepts: Sum of inverse sines equal to π (triangle and sine/cosine rule)
questions.question: For $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\ne0$, if $\sin^{-1}\alpha+\sin^{-1}\beta+\sin^{-1}\gamma=\pi$ and $(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)(\alpha-\gamma+\beta)=3\alpha\beta$, then $\gamma$ equals :
questions.key_idea: Angles $A,B,C$ with $A+B+C=\pi$ and $\sin A=\alpha$ etc. form a triangle whose sides are proportional to $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, so the given relation is the cosine rule for angle $C$.
solution: Because $A,B,C$ are the angles of a triangle (each in $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right]$ as the sum is $\pi$ and each $\le\frac\pi2$) and $\alpha=\sin A,\beta=\sin B,\gamma=\sin C$ are proportional to its sides (sine rule), the left side is $\cos C$.
questions.correction_note: Justification added for the step 'the expression equals $\cos C$' (the PDF states it without saying that $\sin A,\sin B,\sin C$ are proportional to the sides of a triangle with angles $A,B,C$). Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the identity $\sin^2A+\sin^2B-\sin^2C=2\sin A\sin B\cos C$ valid when $A+B+C=\pi$, so no triangle needs to be drawn.
solution: With $A+B+C=\pi$: $\sin^2A-\sin^2C=\sin(A+C)\sin(A-C)=\sin B\sin(A-C)$ and $\sin^2B=\sin B\sin(A+C)$, so $\sin^2A+\sin^2B-\sin^2C=\sin B\left[\sin(A-C)+\sin(A+C)\right]=2\sin A\sin B\cos C$.
The given condition gives $\alpha^2+\beta^2-\gamma^2=\alpha\beta$; with $\alpha\beta\ne0$ this gives $\cos C=\frac12$, so $C=\frac\pi3$.

useful_results: If $A+B+C=\pi$ then $\sin^2A+\sin^2B-\sin^2C=2\sin A\sin B\cos C$ (the cosine rule in sine form).
$\sin^{-1}x_1+\sin^{-1}x_2+\sin^{-1}x_3=\pi$ with $x_i>0$ describes a triangle with circumdiameter $1$ and sides $x_1,x_2,x_3$.
$(a+b)^2-c^2=3ab$ is the signature of $C=60^\circ$ (as $c^2=a^2+b^2-ab$); $(a+b)^2-c^2=ab$ would give $C=120^\circ$.

concepts: Principal values: sin⁻¹(sin x) and cos⁻¹(cos x) for x outside the principal range
questions.question: If $a=\sin^{-1}(\sin5)$ and $b=\cos^{-1}(\cos5)$, then $a^2+b^2$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Reduce $5$ radians into the principal ranges: $\sin^{-1}(\sin5)=5-2\pi$ and $\cos^{-1}(\cos5)=2\pi-5$.
useful_results: $\sin^{-1}(\sin x)$ is the odd, $2\pi$-periodic zig-zag through $(0,0)$, $\left(\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$, $(\pi,0)$, $\left(\frac{3\pi}2,-\frac\pi2\right)$, $(2\pi,0)$.
$\cos^{-1}(\cos x)$ is the even $2\pi$-periodic zig-zag between $0$ and $\pi$; for $x\in[\pi,2\pi]$ it equals $2\pi-x$.
For $x\in\left[\frac{3\pi}2,2\pi\right]$: $\sin^{-1}\sin x=-\cos^{-1}\cos x$ (here $a=-b$).

concepts: Domain of sin⁻¹ of a rational function and of a logarithm
Rational inequalities (wavy curve method)
questions.question: If the domain of the function $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{3x-22}{2x-19}\right)+\log_e\left(\frac{3x^2-8x+5}{x^2-3x-10}\right)$ is $(\alpha,\beta]$, then $3\alpha+10\beta$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Three conditions: $\left|\frac{3x-22}{2x-19}\right|\le1$ (two inequalities) and $\frac{(x-1)(3x-5)}{(x-5)(x+2)}>0$; intersect on a number line.

alternate_solutions.idea: Square the inequality $\left|\frac{3x-22}{2x-19}\right|\le1$ into $(3x-22)^2\le(2x-19)^2$ (a single factorised quadratic), then use sign knowledge on $[3,\frac{41}5]$ so the logarithm condition reduces to one factor.

useful_results: $\left|\frac{P}{Q}\right|\le1\iff(P-Q)(P+Q)\le0$ with $Q\ne0$: one inequality instead of two.
After a first restriction, many factors have a known sign: use it to cut the second inequality to its decisive factor.
Domain of a sum of functions = intersection of the domains; open/closed ends come from log/denominator (open) and inverse trig (closed).

concepts: Properties of cos⁻¹x and sin⁻¹y (range and complementary identity)
Trigonometric identity and minimum of an expression
questions.question: Given that the inverse trigonometric functions take principal values only, let $x,y$ be any two real numbers in $[-1,1]$ such that $\cos^{-1}x-\sin^{-1}y=\alpha$, $-\frac\pi2\le\alpha\le\pi$. Then the minimum value of $x^2+y^2+2xy\sin\alpha$ is :
questions.key_idea: With $x=\cos A,\ y=\sin B$ and $\alpha=A-B$ the expression is exactly $\cos^2\alpha$; its minimum is $0$ at $\alpha=\frac\pi2$.
solution: The minimum value of $\cos^2\alpha$ is $0$, attained at $\alpha=\frac\pi2$ (for example $x=y=0$: $\cos^{-1}0-\sin^{-1}0=\frac\pi2$). Option (D).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes 'cos⁻¹(xy − √(1−x²)√(1−y²)) = π/2 + α', which is true only when $\frac\pi2+\alpha\le\pi$ (for $\alpha\in(\frac\pi2,\pi]$ the sum $\cos^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}y$ exceeds $\pi$). Taking the cosine of both sides avoids this and gives the same relation; attainment of the minimum (x = y = 0) was added. Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Trigonometric substitution $x=\cos A,\ y=\sin B$: the expression collapses to $\cos^2(A-B)$ by the identity $\cos^2A\cos^2B+\sin^2A\sin^2B+2\sin A\cos A\sin B\cos B=(\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B)^2$.
solution: $x^2+y^2+2xy\sin\alpha=\cos^2A+\sin^2B+2\cos A\sin B\left(\sin A\cos B-\cos A\sin B\right)$.
$=\cos^2A\cos^2B+\sin^2A\sin^2B+2\sin A\cos A\sin B\cos B=(\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B)^2=\cos^2(A-B)=\cos^2\alpha$.

useful_results: $\cos^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}y=\frac\pi2+\alpha$: take $\cos$ (not $\cos^{-1}$) of both sides to avoid range issues - the sum of two $\cos^{-1}$'s can exceed $\pi$.
If $\cos^{-1}x-\sin^{-1}y=\alpha$ then $x^2+y^2+2xy\sin\alpha=\cos^2\alpha$; likewise $\cos^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}y=\theta\Rightarrow x^2+y^2-2xy\cos\theta=\sin^2\theta$.
Eliminating the square roots by squaring gives a relation of the form $x^2+y^2-2xy\cos\theta=\sin^2\theta$ (an ellipse in the $xy$ plane): the standard result for two inverse cosines.

concepts: Domain of sin⁻¹ of a rational function (|f| ≤ 1)
questions.question: If the domain of the function $f(x)=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x-1}{2x+3}\right)$ is $\mathbb R-(\alpha,\beta)$, then $12\alpha\beta$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Solve $-1\le\frac{x-1}{2x+3}\le1$ as two rational inequalities and intersect; the gap is $(\alpha,\beta)=\left(-4,-\frac23\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Replace $\left|\frac{x-1}{2x+3}\right|\le1$ by $(x-1)^2\le(2x+3)^2$ and factor the difference of squares.
solution: So $x\le-4$ or $x\ge-\frac23$ (and $x=-\frac32$ lies in the excluded gap anyway).

useful_results: $\left|\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}\right|\le1\iff(ax+b)^2\le(cx+d)^2\iff(ax+b-cx-d)(ax+b+cx+d)\le0$.
The 'complement of an interval' form of the answer comes from the squared inequality having the form $(x-p)(x-q)\ge0$.
The denominator's zero ($x=-\frac32$) lies inside the excluded interval here, so no extra puncture appears.

concepts: Addition of tan⁻¹ terms (cot⁻¹ to tan⁻¹ conversion)
tan(π/4 − θ) formula
questions.question: For $n\in\mathbb N$, if $\cot^{-1}3+\cot^{-1}4+\cot^{-1}5+\cot^{-1}n=\frac\pi4$, then $n$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Convert to $\tan^{-1}\frac1k$, add the three known terms by the tangent-sum formula, and compare $\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\tan^{-1}\frac1n\right)=\frac{n-1}{n+1}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Multiply complex numbers: $\cot^{-1}k=\arg(k+i)$, so the sum of angles is $\arg\left[(3+i)(4+i)(5+i)(n+i)\right]$, and an argument of $\frac\pi4$ means real part $=$ imaginary part.
solution: $\cot^{-1}k=\arg(k+i)$ for $k>0$, and arguments add under multiplication.
The total argument is $\frac\pi4$ (and the sum of four angles is less than $\frac\pi2$, so no extra $\pi$) iff real part $=$ imaginary part: $48n-46=46n+48$.

useful_results: $\cot^{-1}k=\arg(k+i)$ for $k>0$: a sum of $\cot^{-1}$'s is the argument of a product, and the sum is $\frac\pi4$ iff real part $=$ imaginary part of the product.
$\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)=\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$; with $\tan\theta=\frac1n$ it is $\frac{n-1}{n+1}$.

concepts: Range of sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 and number of solutions
questions.question: Let the inverse trigonometric functions take principal values. The number of real solutions of the equation $2\sin^{-1}x+3\cos^{-1}x=\frac{2\pi}5$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Write $2\sin^{-1}x+3\cos^{-1}x=2\left(\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x\right)+\cos^{-1}x=\pi+\cos^{-1}x\ge\pi>\frac{2\pi}5$.
solution: But $\cos^{-1}x\in[0,\pi]$, so there is no real value of $x$.
useful_results: $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\frac\pi2$ for $x\in[-1,1]$: any linear combination $p\sin^{-1}x+q\cos^{-1}x$ reduces to $\frac{p\pi}2+(q-p)\cos^{-1}x$.
Here the left side ranges over $[\pi,2\pi]$ (as $\cos^{-1}x\in[0,\pi]$), so the equation $=c$ has solutions only for $c\in[\pi,2\pi]$.
Always compare the right-hand side with the range of the left side before solving.
